name: intercepting-validator
intent: Insert one interception layer on the ingress path that validates every inbound message before any handler runs, so that input checking is uniform, central and impossible to forget per endpoint.
problem: Inbound data - HTTP requests, RPC messages, queue events, protocol frames - is validated inside each handler: every new endpoint re-implements parsing, range and encoding checks, rules drift between handlers, and some paths end up with no validation at all. The recurring decision is where to put validation so that all inbound data passes through it exactly once, before application logic.
context: Request- or message-driven systems with a well-defined ingress - HTTP APIs, RPC services, queue consumers, protocol front ends - where several handlers accept external data, where shared constraints (schema, ranges, encodings, size limits) can be expressed without loading domain state, and where the ingress pipeline (filter chain, middleware stack, plugin pipeline, responder chain) can be owned and configured by the team.
benefits: Validation coverage becomes structural: a new endpoint or message type inherits the checks by being wired into the same pipeline instead of by remembering to copy validation code.
One place to change the rules: a changed constraint (maximum length, encoding policy, forbidden patterns) is edited once and applies uniformly to every ingress path.
Handlers simplify: they may assume a validated, canonical shape and contain only application logic, with no defensive parsing, and rejection responses stay uniform across the surface.
Testability: validators are units with one contract (accept or reject with a reason), so the rule set and the layer can be exercised against adversarial corpora without booting handlers.
Cheap mechanical checks (size, type, ranges, encodings) are enforced at the boundary before any resource is allocated or any handler is entered.
tradeoffs: Completeness is load-bearing: the guarantee holds only while every path into the system crosses the layer; one bypass (admin endpoint, batch import, direct service call, test harness) silently voids it, so the layer must be audited for coverage, not merely installed.
Ordering coupling: validation semantics become a function of chain order, and reordering a filter/middleware changes outcomes far away from the handler that consumes the data.
Hot-path cost: every message pays parse and rule evaluation even when the handler would never touch the offending field; expensive validators need caching, cheap-first ordering or short-circuiting.

Lowest-common-denominator rules: an interception layer enforces envelope-level and shared invariants well, but contextual, type-specific or state-dependent rules still belong elsewhere, which duplicates some logic or forces a second validation pass.

Framework lock-in of the interception API: filters, middleware, plugins and interceptors are framework- and transport-specific, so the layer is reimplemented on a framework or transport change and often needs the framework's test harness unless validation is extracted into pure functions.

False confidence: validating shape is not authorising - teams that route everything through the layer may under-check authorization and privilege - and boundary checks duplicated by downstream typed parsing are wasted work.

participants.responsibility: The single pipeline position through which every inbound message must pass before any handler; owns the chain's existence and ordering.
Runs the ordered validators for each message, stops at the first rejection, and routes accepted (canonical) data to the handler.
One small, side-effect-free rule that inspects a message (schema, ranges, encodings, size) and returns accept or a rejection reason.
The shared, declarative definition of what valid inbound data is (schema, limits, forbidden values) that validators execute.
Application logic that consumes only validated data and contains no defensive input parsing of its own.
Turns a failed validation into the uniform error contract and records the event (audit/logging) without leaking raw input.

use_cases: A public REST or GraphQL API where every request body and query parameter must pass schema, range and size validation before any controller is invoked.
A message-queue consumer that validates every inbound event against its schema and version before dispatching it to a handler.
A file or protocol ingest pipeline (CSV, XML, binary frames) that validates frames in one front layer before domain processing begins.
A multi-tenant service that enforces tenant-scoped constraints uniformly - allowed fields, payload caps, encoding policy - on all inbound requests.
An RPC or WebSocket gateway that rejects non-conforming request messages with one error format before they reach service handlers.
A GraphQL API gateway that validates incoming query operations for schema conformance, depth limits and argument types at the boundary before query execution begins.
A gRPC service fronted by a protobuf interceptor that enforces proto-schema type and structural constraints on all inbound RPC requests before they reach the service implementation.
A FastAPI service that attaches a shared Depends() dependency to an APIRouter and uses Pydantic request models so invalid requests are rejected before the path operation.
An ASP.NET Core application that places request validation in the middleware pipeline or a Minimal API endpoint filter, short-circuiting with a problem response before the endpoint delegate.
An Express application that mounts schema-validation middleware on a router before its routes, returning a 4xx response without calling next() when the request is invalid.
avoid_when: There is a single entry point or one handler: plain guard clauses inside that function (guard-clause) are simpler than constructing a pipeline.
The rules need loaded domain state or aggregates to evaluate: place them with the domain (specification, assertion) instead of forcing state access into the boundary layer.

The ingress is already a strict generated parser (typed RPC, protobuf, machine-checked schema) that makes malformed input unreachable; then only semantic checks remain and they belong with the domain.
Latency is so tight that a per-message generic rule engine dominates the budget, and validation at the source or inside the zero-copy parser is the only acceptable cost.
anti_patterns: Validation as the only defence: treating the layer as if it also authorised requests or enforced state-dependent invariants; it is a boundary filter, not a reference monitor.
Partial coverage by accident: wiring the main HTTP route through the layer while admin APIs, CLI entry points and batch imports reach the same services unvalidated.
God validator: one interceptor that parses, validates, transforms, authorises and audits, so every change ripples and the layer becomes untestable.
Validation theatre: checking only convenient shapes (types) while ignoring encodings, sizes and canonical forms, or trusting client-side validation as if it were the boundary check.
Order by accident: registering validators without tests that pin precedence, so a refactor silently reorders rejection behaviour.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: ingress policy (validation) is separated from application behaviour (handlers own only domain logic).
Single point of definition (DRY): shared constraints are declared once and executed by one layer instead of being re-expressed per handler.
Complete mediation: every inbound datum is checked, not just the first one on a path - a guarantee, not a best effort.
Fail-safe defaults: input that cannot be validated (missing rule set, validator exception, unknown encoding) is rejected rather than passed through.
Separation of mechanism from policy: the pipeline is the mechanism, the rule set is the replaceable policy.
best_practices: Keep validators small, deterministic and side-effect-free - one rule per validator with a shared accept/reject contract - so rules compose and are unit-testable in isolation.
Pin chain order with tests and documentation; make registration explicit and reviewable so precedence is a decision, not an accident.
Validate once at the boundary and canonicalise there (normalise encodings, types, whitespace) so handlers consume exactly one representation.
Give failures a uniform contract (stable error shape with field paths) and log or audit rejections without echoing raw input back to the caller.
Extract rule logic into framework-independent functions; the pipeline hook should be a thin adapter so rules can be tested without the framework.
Enforce coverage: assert that every registered route or consumer passes through the layer (pipeline introspection or a route-table test) and fail the build when one does not.
Fail closed: if the layer itself cannot evaluate a message, reject it rather than silently letting it through.

Emit structured error responses conforming to RFC 7807 (application/problem+json) so API clients receive machine-readable `type`, `title`, `detail` and `instance` URIs regardless of which validator rejected the request.

Use schema-first or contract-first workflows (OpenAPI, JSON Schema, protobuf) to generate validators from a canonical type definition rather than hand-writing validation logic, keeping the schema the single source of truth.

Test the validator layer itself with adversarial corpora including boundary values, malformed encodings and ReDoS-crafted inputs; automate these as a CI gate rather than running them only during security review.
sources: Markus Schumacher, Eduardo Fernandez-Buglioni, Duane Hybertson, Frank Buschmann, Peter Sommerlad, Security Patterns: Integrating Security and Systems Engineering, Wiley (2006) - security pattern catalog with the Intercepting Validator in the request security pipeline; cited as the §8 provenance in docs/design-patterns.md.

OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet — authoritative guidance on allowlist vs denylist validation, regex safety (ReDoS awareness), syntactic vs semantic validation, and server-side-first validation strategy. https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html

OWASP Top 10 Proactive Controls 2024, Control C3: Validate All Input & Handle Exceptions — codifies input validation as a mandatory top-tier security control, directly motivating the intercepting-validator pattern as its primary implementation strategy. https://top10proactive.owasp.org/the-top-10/c3-validate-input-and-handle-exceptions

RFC 7807 — Problem Details for HTTP APIs — IETF standard defining a machine-readable error format (`application/problem+json`) with `type`, `title`, `detail`, `status`, and `instance` members; directly applicable to the pattern's uniform rejection-handler error contract.

CWE-20 Improper Input Validation — MITRE Common Weakness Enumeration entry for the class of vulnerabilities the intercepting-validator pattern prevents; useful for severity benchmarking and compliance framework mapping. https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/20.html
